title: The wind
hook: on a freezing night of the siege, Hudhayfah crosses to the enemy camp, holds his arrow, and the wind scatters the confederate armies (33:9; Muslim)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Trench: a call and an answer across a ditch, and Jabir's small pot that fed everyone. Your line was: dig together. Did you work next to someone, not instead of them? Day seven hundred eighty-three.

Who will go and bring me news of the enemy? The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ asks it of his companions on a bitter night of the siege. The trench has held, but the armies are still camped on the far side, and the siege drags on. Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman remembers this night in Sahih Muslim. No one answers. The Prophet asks again. Silence. He asks a third time. Still no one stands up. Today: the wind.
screen: `WHO WILL BRING ME NEWS?` → `A BITTER NIGHT OF THE SIEGE.` → `NO ONE ANSWERS.`

segments.voice: Then the Prophet calls one man by name: get up, Hudhayfah. And Hudhayfah says that once he was named, he had no choice. The Prophet gives him two instructions. Bring me news of them. And don't stir them up against me. So he goes, alone, across the dark. And here's the strange part of his telling: on the way, he felt as if he were walking in a warm bath. He reaches the enemy camp and sees Abu Sufyan, the Meccan commander, warming his back at a fire. Hudhayfah fits an arrow to his bow. He wants to shoot. He says he would have hit him. And then he remembers: don't stir them up. He lowers the bow. He walks back, still warm, and gives his report, and the moment he's done, the cold comes back. The Prophet wraps him in a spare cloak he used for prayer, and Hudhayfah sleeps there until morning, when the Prophet wakes him: get up, sleeper. Meanwhile, the camp he had walked through was coming apart. Surah al-Ahzab remembers it in Pickthall's words: "O ye who believe! Remember Allah's favour unto you when there came against you hosts, and We sent against them a great wind and hosts ye could not see." The biographers say the wind knocked over pots and blew out fires, and the armies packed up and left. In Bukhari, the Prophet says afterward: now we will go to them, and they will not come to us. Notice what Hudhayfah did not do. The one dramatic act within his reach, he held back. The ending didn't come from his arrow. In the Qur'an's telling, it came from the wind.
screen: `GET UP, HUDHAYFAH.` · `DON'T STIR THEM UP.` · `THE ARROW HELD BACK.` · `A GREAT WIND AND HOSTS YE COULD NOT SEE.` · then, large: `THE WIND CAME.`

segments.voice: The practice: wait out a storm. Sit, and let the breath slow. Think of something you're under siege from right now: a conflict, a worry, a stretch of waiting. Notice the arrow in your hand: the angry email, the sharp word, the move that would feel good for one second and stir everything up. Don't fire it. Just hold it, the way Hudhayfah held his. Notice what it's like to wait instead. If you pray, you can recite "hasbunallahu wa ni'mal wakil", Allah is enough for us, and the best guardian, the words of 3:173. If you don't, simply rest, and let the storm be the storm. The bell holds the time.
The wind: the great wind of Surah al-Ahzab that broke up the armies around Medina, on the night Hudhayfah held his arrow. Today's word.
Your line: the wind came. Today, when you're tempted to fire off the one thing that would stir things up, hold it, and wait a little longer. Day seven hundred eighty-three.

howItsDone: Muslims recite the opening of the Confederates passage, 33:9 onward, as a reminder of rescue under siege, and the phrase hasbunallahu wa ni'mal wakil is said by some in hard times.

fork.setup: you're Hudhayfah, alone in the enemy camp at night. the Meccan commander is warming himself at a fire, within range. what do you do?
options: shoot; this could end the siege.
lower the bow and go back with your report.

fork.reveal: he wanted to shoot, but remembered the Prophet's order: don't stir them up. he lowered the bow. the wind ended the siege.

original.note: Arabic: wind; the Qur'an uses the word in 33:9 for the wind sent against the confederate armies.

trapdoor: what you thought: a lucky storm.
what it means: a siege that ended not by an arrow, but by a wind the Qur'an calls Allah's favor.
what a scholar hears: 33:9's wind and unseen hosts, Hudhayfah's night in Muslim 1788, and Bukhari's 'now we will go to them'.

notes: Pickthall 33:9 quoted from memory; confirm exact wording, including 'favour' and 'hosts ye could not see'.
Muslim 1788 retold from memory; confirm the details: the question asked three times, 'don't stir them up', the warmth like a bath, Abu Sufyan at the fire, the cloak, 'qum ya nawman'.
'He asks a third time' depends on Muslim 1788's wording; confirm the count of the Prophet's question.
The siege's length is left vague ('drags on') under the claims rule.
The practice offers 'hasbunallahu wa ni'mal wakil' (3:173), an existing Qur'anic phrase, not a new prayer; howItsDone says it 'is said by some in hard times'.
Year 1 day 268 mentioned the wind briefly; this day centers on Hudhayfah's night.

Editor: the hook now opens on the Prophet's question instead of a second cold-weather opener right after day 782's 'a cold morning'; cut the narrator's guess at the companions' reasons ('too cold, too dark, too far'), which Muslim 1788 does not give. Screen updated to match.
